name: Wendy Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stock hand at Hartley Farm, which runs about a hundred and forty suckler cows. That means the cows raise their own calves, and we sell the calves on for beef at about ten months. In summer we make hay and silage off two hundred acres, and in winter it's feeding, bedding and checking the cattle in the sheds twice a day. I'm out by seven, back for the school run at half three if Craig can't do it, and back out again for the evening check.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at it, and what came before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eighteen months. Before that I was a cashier at the bank in town for twenty years, until they shut the branch and told us to apply for jobs in a call centre an hour away. I'd always helped my uncle with his cattle at weekends, so when Hartley's needed someone, I jumped. I'm still green, I've only done one calving season, but I'm learning fast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that nobody's watching a screen to count how fast I serve customers. I like the calves, and I like haymaking, the smell of it, even when the baler breaks for the third time in a day. What wears me out is the money. It's less than the bank, Craig's a plasterer and work's up and down, and we've got a mortgage and two kids who eat like cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use it, it's handy. I use it every day, for the herd records, for working out feed rations, for writing the ads when we sell hay. I'd tell anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's my secret weapon. I'm a beginner at forty-three, and it lets me ask a hundred stupid questions without anyone knowing. My boss, Phil, thinks I've been farming for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push it further. I'd set up proper records for each cow on the farm, weights, calving dates, which ones need help, so Phil can see which cows to keep. I'd also start selling small hay bales online to horse owners, I reckon there's two thousand a year in it for the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite cheerful. It suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the money from that hay come to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, that's the next conversation. I'd go to Phil with the numbers and ask for a cut, ten percent maybe. He's fair, but he won't offer it unless I ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Phil thinks you've been farming for years. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If he ever asks me something on the spot in the yard, I'm stuck, because my phone's in the truck. But mostly I'm catching up for real, the tool just speeds it along.

S0.say: I'd say use it, it's handy. I use it every day for herd records, feed rations and hay adverts, and I'd tell anyone who'd listen.
S0.think: It's my secret weapon as a beginner at forty-three, because I can ask a hundred stupid questions without anyone knowing. Phil thinks I've been farming for years.
S0.do: Sets up proper records for each cow so the farm can choose which to keep. Starts selling small hay bales online to horse owners, about two thousand a year, and asks for a ten percent cut.
S0.quote: It lets me ask a hundred stupid questions without anyone knowing.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy is brisk and thinks in numbers, a habit from twenty years at a bank counter. She uses AI to hide how new she is, and admits that has a weak spot when her phone is in the truck. She's already spotting small money-making ideas for the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible, gives everyone time. Bit harsh on youngsters, but they'll adapt. Most people panic too early about these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, slow suits me fine, because I'm quick with the tools and I've got time to get ahead. I've already watched one industry do this, the bank, and slow is much better than what happened there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Phil a small direct-sales scheme, boxes of beef sold to local families, using AI for the website and the orders. Maybe twenty boxes a month to start. If it works, I'd ask to run it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me what happened at the bank.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They didn't sack us in one go. They cut the hours, then the opening days, then the counter staff, over about six years. By the end there were three of us and a queue of pensioners who couldn't use the app. That's the version of slow I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Craig say about beef boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say who's doing the deliveries, and look at me. Then he'd do them on Saturdays, because he's soft. He'd moan the whole time and love it.

S1.say: I'd say it's sensible and gives everyone time. It's a bit harsh on young people, but most people panic too early.
S1.think: Slow suits me, because I'm quick with the tools and I'd get ahead. I've already lived through a slow version of this at the bank, and slow is better than fast.
S1.do: Pitches a small beef box scheme to local families, with an AI-built website and orders, starting at about twenty boxes a month. Asks to run it properly if it works.
S1.quote: By the end there were three of us and a queue of pensioners who couldn't use the app. That's the version of slow I know.
S1.fieldNote: Her bank experience is central: she's seen slow cuts before and isn't scared of them. Her instinct is to start something new rather than defend what she has. Her centre outlook shows in calling the scenario sensible and cautioning against panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what happened to banks ten years ago, now it's everyone else's turn. Make sure there's retraining, sure, but don't stop it. Some people will do very well out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be one of the people who does well, on a small scale. I know both sides, the office and the farm. Every farm round here has paperwork piling up, and I could be the one who sorts it with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer a paperwork service to neighbouring farms, cattle movement records, subsidy forms, the passport for every animal, on two evenings a week at maybe twenty-five an hour. I'd tell Phil first so he doesn't hear it from someone else. I'd keep the stock job, that's the safe bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some people will do very well. Who loses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old colleagues at the bank call centre, probably, the ones who took the jobs an hour away. Janice is still there, she's fifty-six. I'd feel bad, but honestly, I'd also send her my number in case she wanted to do farm paperwork with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two evenings on top of the farm. What gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleep, mostly. And the gym membership I never use, that's thirty a month back straight away. Ellie's sixteen, she can cook twice a week, it's good for her.

S2.say: I'd say this happened to banks ten years ago and now it's everyone else's turn. Retrain people, but don't stop it, because some will do very well.
S2.think: I'd be one of the people who does well, on a small scale, because I know the office and the farm. Every farm round here has paperwork piling up, and I could sort it with AI.
S2.do: Offers a farm paperwork service to neighbours two evenings a week at about twenty-five an hour, telling Phil first. Keeps the stock job as the safe base and cancels a thirty pound gym membership.
S2.quote: I'd feel bad, but honestly, I'd also send her my number in case she wanted to do farm paperwork with me.
S2.fieldNote: She is the rare person who sees the office scenario as an opening, because she sits between two worlds. She thought about a former colleague still in the call centre, then turned it into a business idea, which is very much her. She plans to take time from sleep and her teenage daughter's help, without much hesitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to share the gains somehow, but not by wrecking everything. Maybe a tax on the very top, help for people retraining. I'm not for either extreme, I'd say that loudly, which nobody likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved to be in cattle, not in the bank. Hands-on work is safe in that picture. But my paperwork sideline might get eaten, if AI matches skilled people, the farmers can just ask it themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the paperwork idea and go hard on the beef boxes, because people with booming house prices like buying local meat. I'd try to get Phil to let me rent ten cows of my own on his land. It's a gamble, I'd need a loan of about eight thousand, which scares me with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited anxious, the good kind mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Eight thousand with under a month saved. Talk me through that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, I know. I'd only do it if Phil would let me pay him back in calves rather than cash, which farmers do. If it went wrong we'd lose the car, not the house. That's my line: never the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should get the gains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who did the work, a bit, and people who lost out, a bit more. But I don't trust anyone who says they've got the perfect answer. Everyone at the pub has a perfect answer and none of them agree.

S3.say: I'd say the government should share the gains without wrecking everything, maybe a tax on the very top and help with retraining. I'm not for either extreme, and I'd say that loudly.
S3.think: I'd be relieved to be in cattle and not in the bank. But my paperwork sideline might vanish, because farmers could just ask the AI themselves.
S3.do: Drops the paperwork idea and pushes the beef boxes to buyers flush from house prices. Asks Phil to let her keep ten cows of her own on his land, borrowing about eight thousand and paying him back in calves.
S3.feel: Anxious, but mostly the good, excited kind.
S3.quote: If it went wrong we'd lose the car, not the house. That's my line: never the house.
S3.fieldNote: She kept moving to the next opportunity as the old one closed, which is her adaptability in action. When I pushed on borrowing with thin savings, she had a clear limit: the car can go, the house can't. She was openly sceptical of anyone with a perfect answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms are coming whether we like it or not, so let's make sure local people run them. Training, grants for small farms, not just the big ones. I'd say it at the farmers' union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my stock job is at risk. Feeding, bedding, even checking cattle with cameras, a robot could do a lot of it. What it can't do yet is calve a heifer at two in the morning in a storm, but I'm not sure how long yet lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Phil to let me be the robot person, learn to set them up and fix them, before he hires someone from outside. I'd put everything into the beef boxes and my own cows, because people will pay more for meat they know a person raised. I'd use AI to learn the robot side every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed. I'd keep moving so I didn't have time to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people will pay more for meat a person raised. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not sure. I'm betting. When the bank went to apps, the posh coffee shop on the high street got busier, people wanted a face. I think meat might go the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ellie and Josh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That their mum's been here before, at the bank, and came out of it into a job she loves. Ellie would roll her eyes. Josh would ask if he could drive the robot.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms are coming, so make sure local people run them, with training and grants for small farms. I'd say it at the farmers' union meeting.
S4.think: My stock job is at risk, because a robot could feed, bed and watch the cattle. It can't calve a heifer at two in the morning yet, but I don't know how long yet lasts.
S4.do: Asks Phil to make her the person who sets up and fixes the robots before he hires from outside. Puts everything into beef boxes and her own cows, and studies robots with AI each night.
S4.feel: Anxious, close to alarmed, and keeping busy so she can't panic.
S4.quote: What it can't do yet is calve a heifer at two in the morning in a storm, but I'm not sure how long yet lasts.
S4.fieldNote: Her mood rose but didn't hit alarm, because she has several plans already moving. She openly called her bet on hand-raised meat a bet, with a real example from the bank closure. She copes by staying busy, and seemed to know that about herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because it's the only one where my plans run out. What would help is small loans for people like me to buy a few cows or a share of a robot, so it's not only the big farms that get them. And a training course that's evenings, because I can't stop working to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people who've already lost a job to a machine. I have. You don't get over it by complaining, you get over it by finding the next thing. I wish someone had asked me that at the bank.

headlineQuote: What it can't do yet is calve a heifer at two in the morning in a storm, but I'm not sure how long yet lasts.
portrait: Wendy Fischer is 43 and has been a stock hand on a suckler beef and hay farm for eighteen months, after twenty years as a bank cashier until her branch shut. She lives with Craig, a plasterer, and their two teenagers, with a mortgage and almost no savings. She uses AI every day and treats each scenario as a business problem, from hay sales and beef boxes to a farm paperwork service and renting cows of her own. She has already lost one job to technology and refuses to panic, though the robot scenario is where she admits her plans start to run out.
biggestWorry: The robots scenario, because it's the only one where her plans run out and her stock job is at risk.
whatWouldHelp: Small loans so people like her can buy a few cows or a share of a robot, and evening training courses she can do while working.
